name: Reddish Grey
lede: Reddish grey is a grey with a warm red cast, a plain description that old color lists and painting manuals both rely on.

sections.title: An old entry in the grey list
sections.body:
The phrase appears in Baty's color book in the introductory lists of named shades, where it sits among the greys with ash-grey, pearl-grey, lead-grey and steel-grey [1]. The same lists sort whites, blacks and blues by the same method: a base word plus a tint word [1]. Reddish-grey there names a neutral by its slight lean [1].

On the chart side, the modern swatch matches the ISCC-NBS block for a light reddish brown, a reminder of how close a warm grey sits to brown [2]. Its sibling neutrals are [[grey]], [[brownish-grey]] and [[pearl-grey]].

sections.title: A grey for the painter's palette
sections.body: Gurney, writing on color and light for painters, gives a practical use: mix up a supply of pink or reddish gray and weave it in among the greens of a landscape [3]. He credits the landscape painter Stapleton Kearns with the method, which Kearns calls smuggling reds [3]. A warm neutral helps a large green area avoid monotony [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: It appears in 169 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.71 per cent, holding at least five per cent of the canvas [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, found in 22 of 1,674 paintings, which is 2.9 times the rate those museums would predict [4]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 59 per cent of the 93 paintings found by the within-painting search [4]. Maurice Denis is the most devoted painter, with it in 4 of his 43 works here [4]. A top example is Degas's [[painting:commons-Q76424023|Dancers practicing in the Foyer]], where the color covers about 43 per cent of the canvas [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so they show how a picture looks now, not what the painter mixed [4].
